stories.headline: Both sides of the contract divide between Karl-Anthony Towns and the Knicks
stories.summary: KAT and the Knicks are far apart on extension talks. ESPN insiders break down each side, plus project where this saga is headed.
stories.body:
Karl-Anthony Towns has repeatedly stated his goal is a new deal to remain with the New York Knicks.

And since the NBA Finals concluded in June, Towns has been eligible for one: a four-year, $276 million contract extension that would keep him with the defending champs through the 2030-31 season. However, as sources told ESPN's Shams Charania, the Knicks' latest offer to Towns was a four-year deal worth approximately $200 million.

The reason: A max contract for the 30-year-old All-Star center would introduce major second apron concerns, a space Knicks owner James Dolan has shown no interest in occupying. Towns, for his part, says he is willing to meet somewhere in the middle.

"I want to do something that can keep the team together and work with the Knicks and also values me," Towns said Monday. "None of those things have come close to happening."

Will the Knicks enter opening night without getting a deal done? How hard should Towns push in negotiations? What options would be available next summer?

ESPN NBA insiders Ben Golliver, Zach Kram and Bobby Marks examine both sides of the Towns-Knicks contract talks -- plus the deal our resident general manager would choose.

Breaking down Towns' case for more money

Towns has every reason to push hard in these negotiations. Recent history suggests that teams basking in the championship afterglow almost always do what it takes to financially reward their core players.

Although Jalen Brunson and OG Anunoby outperformed Towns in the NBA Finals, the Knicks should view the 7-footer as an indispensable part of their title formula. Without Towns to space the floor, New York's Brunson-led offense wouldn't be as effective. Without Towns stepping up defensively against Victor Wembanyama -- the San Antonio Spurs star was held well below his regular-season field goal and 3-point shooting percentages in the series -- New York likely wouldn't have waltzed to a five-game Finals victory. And without Towns, the Knicks would be stuck with Andre Drummond as their best remaining center.

That feels like a decent amount of leverage.

Towns inked a four-year, $220.4 million extension with the Minnesota Timberwolves in 2022 that covered his late 20s. While that deal looked questionable at the time, the Timberwolves were able to recoup solid value when they traded him to the Knicks in 2024, and he delivered a 2025 All-NBA selection before serving as a vital part of the 2026 title team. Towns' availability in New York has also been excellent: He has appeared in 90% of the Knicks' regular-season games and all their playoff games the past two seasons.

Philadelphia 76ers center Joel Embiid signed a three-year, $193 million extension in 2024 -- an overly generous agreement that has aged poorly due to his repeated injuries. Towns doesn't deserve to be in that ballpark because he's not being paid to be New York's franchise player. But Towns can argue that he is a more accomplished player than Miami Heat center Bam Adebayo (three-year, $166 million extension in 2024) and Cleveland Cavaliers big man Evan Mobley (five-year, $269 million extension in 2024). And at 30, Towns shouldn't suffer major age-related decline until the latter stages of his next contract.

A four-year, $220 million extension would give Towns a higher AAV than Adebayo and Mobley and a significantly lower AAV than Nikola Jokic, Anthony Davis, Giannis Antetokounmpo and Embiid. Meeting at $220 million would also provide the Knicks with real savings under his four-year, $276 million maximum extension number. -- Golliver

Breaking down New York's case for a discount

Towns has the right to negotiate for every penny, and he should, after helping the Knicks win their first championship in 53 years. But New York's reported four-year offer in the range of $200 million is in the right ballpark for a player of his age and skill set, even if it would represent a pay cut for Towns, whose previous four-year deal was for $220.4 million.

The former No. 1 pick is an excellent player, but he's not in the top tier of NBA superstars.

Towns has three third-team All-NBA nods on his résumé, but no first- or second-team appearances, suggesting he never has been a top-10 player in the league. And that's unlikely to change now that he is presumably at or past his individual peak. (Towns turns 31 next month.)

Moreover, Towns' leap in the 2025-26 postseason came more as a role player than a max-level star. He ranked third on the Knicks in playoff points per game, behind Brunson and Anunoby, and his playoff usage rate was a near-average 20.6%. It's difficult to pay a role player -- even an elite role player with star upside -- upward of $50 million per season in the current salary cap environment.

Coincidentally, the DARKO projection system estimates Towns was worth $52.8 million last season. Factoring in the rising cap on one hand and the typical aging curve on the other, four more years at a $50 million average seems about right. -- Kram

Options if Towns enters 2026-27 without an extension

Towns not signing an extension by Oct. 19 would not mean the window has closed. Because he is technically in the final year of his contract, Towns is eligible to sign a four-year extension through June 30. A lack of an extension before the regular season, however, would leave Towns with five options next summer:

Pick up the $61 million player option for 2027-28, then sign a new long-term deal with New York starting in 2028-29.
Decline the option, then sign a new contract with New York at a salary lower than the $61 million option but with future guaranteed money.
Become a free agent. Teams with projected cap space include the Atlanta Hawks, Brooklyn Nets, Chicago Bulls, Golden State Warriors, LA Clippers, Memphis Grizzlies, Milwaukee Bucks and Sacramento Kings. No free agent has switched teams and signed for more than $49 million in the first season since Paul George's four-year, $212 million max contract with the Philadelphia 76ers in 2024.
Work on a sign-and-trade. Because the Knicks would be the sending team, they would be allowed to exceed the first apron (but not the second) in such a deal.
Pick up his player option and request a trade.

-- Marks

Towns' best path: Opt in, then sign a new contract in 2027

In the scenarios listed above, declining the player option in favor of a new deal would result in Towns essentially signing for $140 million to $160 million. However, picking up the option and then signing a four-year, $180 million extension that starts in 2028-29 would secure more guaranteed money.

And a $40 million cap hit in 2028-29 would accomplish Dolan's goal to remain below the second apron -- even after a max-level contract for Brunson and a new deal for Josh Hart. (Even with Towns' $61 million, New York could still avoid the second apron next season if it declines the team option of Pacome Dadiet and likely renounces 2027 free agent Miles McBride.) -- Marks

stories.headline: George Russell's F1 engine nightmare to continue with Singapore GP grid penalty - sources
stories.summary: George Russell is set to start Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix from the back of the grid as a knock-on effect of his engine failure at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, sources have told ESPN.
stories.body:
George Russell is set to start Sunday's Singapore Grand Prix from the back of the grid as a knock-on effect of his engine failure at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, sources have told ESPN.

The Mercedes driver retired from third place at Sepang due to a mechanical failure with six laps to go, delivering a critical blow to his title chances as teammate Kimi Antonelli extended his championship lead to 84 points.

The failure means Mercedes will need to introduce a new power unit to Russell's car at this weekend's Singapore Grand Prix, sources have told ESPN, taking the British driver over his quota of power unit components for the season and resulting in a grid penalty.

As a cost-saving measure in F1's regulations, each car is only allowed a set number of power unit components for the season, with additional usage resulting in grid drops at the next grand prix.

After reliability issues earlier this year, Mercedes had already planned for Russell to take an additional power unit before the end of the season but was not planning for him to do so in Singapore where overtaking is notoriously difficult.

However, the failure in Malaysia has forced the team's hand as Russell does not have enough sufficiently low-mileage parts in his pool of power unit components to avoid taking a fresh engine this weekend.

- Singapore Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch

- Bahrain GP was the worst indictment of F1's new engine regs yet

- Could Malaysia return to F1 calendar? The state of play

Mercedes is set to bring a performance upgrade to its power unit before the end of the year, which it had originally hoped to coincide with the introduction of Russell's final power unit of the year.

The team has not yet confirmed whether the upgrade -- granted under the FIA's Additional Development Upgrade Opportunity (ADUO) catch-up mechanism -- can be fast-tracked for introduction in Singapore.

If it is not possible to use the ADUO upgrade in Singapore, Mercedes will then face the decision of whether to take a further grid penalty with Russell later in the year to put the upgraded power unit in his car.

Antonelli has already used one additional power unit beyond his season-long quota, which resulted in a grid penalty at the Italian Grand Prix. Despite starting 19th at Monza, the championship leader went on to win the race.

stories.body:
SC Freiburg striker Igor Matanovic has Manchester United, Arsenal and Chelsea on his trail, while Atlético Madrid and Juventus are monitoring Arsenal winger Noni Madueke with a view to a loan move. Join us for the latest transfer news and rumors from around the globe.

- Manchester United are tracking SC Freiburg striker Igor Matanovic alongside Arsenal and Chelsea, TEAMtalk reports. The 23-year-old Croatia international has 21 goals in 57 games for the club and his transfer is valued at €60 million, with United keen to bolster up front amid Benjamin Sesko's ongoing injury issues. Arsenal could move on Viktor Gyökeres, while Chelsea have identified him as a backup option to João Pedro.

- Atlético Madrid and Juventus are monitoring Arsenal winger Noni Madueke with a view to a potential January loan move, according to The Telegraph. The 33-year-old, who has scored 152 goals and provided 34 assists in 154 matches for the club, is set to commit his future to the Allianz Arena despite previous links with Barcelona.

The 20-year-old Brazil international, who has also been linked with Roma, remains highly regarded by the Spanish club despite his frustration over a lack of minutes.

- AC Milan are planning a January approach for Manchester United striker Joshua Zirkzee, per Calciomercato. The Rossoneri hope to agree an initial loan deal with an option to sign permanently for the 25-year-old to complete an attacking line featuring Gonçalo Ramos and Francesco Camarda.

stories.headline: NHL Tonight: Get ready for Round 1 of the Battle of New York
stories.summary: Rangers-Islanders is the marquee matchup on the NHL's nine-game slate. Here's what to watch in each contest.
stories.body:
Following a light four-game slate on Monday, the NHL is quite busy on Tuesday night. There are nine games on the calendar, including the first matchup of the season between the rival New York Islanders and New York Rangers.

Later, the Vegas Golden Knights take on the surprisingly high-scoring Seattle Kraken, and the Florida Panthers close out their West Coast trip with a visit to the Los Angeles Kings.

Here's what to watch in each contest:

Odds are provided by DraftKings and subject to change.

Carolina Hurricanes at Montreal Canadiens

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | CAR -125, O/U: 6.5

It's a rematch of the 2026 Eastern Conference finals, won 4-1 by the Hurricanes. Neither team has gotten off to a perfect start, but both are expected to again be near the top of the conference throughout the season and come playoff time, when it matters most.

Nashville Predators at Toronto Maple Leafs

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | TOR -155, O/U: 5.5

In another version of reality, Markham, Ontario, native Steven Stamkos would have played for the Maple Leafs at some point in his career. As it stands, all 625 of his career goals have been scored for the Lightning or Predators -- including seven against the Maple Leafs in Toronto. On the other side, Auston Matthews had a fun time the last occasion the Preds were in town, scoring two goals in a 7-4 win.

Ottawa Senators at Detroit Red Wings

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | OTT -105, O/U: 5.5

After a chaotic summer, the Red Wings haven't won a game yet this season, but maybe the third time will be the charm. The visiting Senators will do their part to continue Detroit's losing ways. Newly minted captain Thomas Chabot has been a particular bright spot, tied for the team lead in scoring and playing his usual ridiculous amount of minutes (27:06 average ice time per game).

Utah Mammoth at New Jersey Devils

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | NJ -135, O/U: 5.5

Following a 4-2 loss to the Rangers on Sunday, the Mammoth cross the Hudson River into the Garden State to try their luck against another Metro Division foe. The Devils had the Mammoth's number last season, winning both games (2-1 on Dec. 19 and 4-1 on Jan. 3).

Minnesota Wild at Buffalo Sabres

7 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | MIN -108, O/U: 6.5

The Wild's superstar duo of Quinn Hughes and Kirill Kaprizov has delivered this season; both have three points through two games heading into this showdown in western New York. Not to be outdone, Buffalo's Owen Power has gotten off to a hot start as well, with three assists through the Sabres' opening two contests.

New York Islanders at New York Rangers

7:30 p.m. ET (ESPN) | NYR -142, O/U: 5.5

One of the NHL's most storied rivalries takes center stage as the Isles pay a visit to Madison Square Garden. The two clubs have met 340 times in their histories, and the Rangers hold the all-time series lead 161-150-19-10. The Islanders have won five of the eight playoff series between the clubs, though the teams have not squared off since 1994.

The game could also feature a matchup between two of the league's elite netminders -- the Rangers' Igor Shesterkin and the Islanders' Ilya Sorokin -- who have been friends since they were 16 (and Sorokin is godfather to Shesterkin's son, Timofey).

St. Louis Blues at Chicago Blackhawks

8 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | STL -135, O/U: 5.5

The Blues-Blackhawks rivalry might be a little lower on the priority list, but this one gets hot when both teams are contending. The teams have split their past two playoff series (Blackhawks won 4-2 in 2014, while the Blues won 4-3 in 2016). In 2026, the Blackhawks are still searching for their first win of the campaign, but perhaps there's extra motivation to earn it against this old Norris Division foe.

Vegas Golden Knights at Seattle Kraken

9 p.m. ET (ESPN+) | VGK -166, O/U: 5.5

One of the more surprising stats of the 2026-27 season is that the Kraken are sixth in the NHL in goals per game (4.33) after finishing 28th last season (2.73). Some early momentum would be nice for a team that has struggled to make it back to the playoffs, having missed out the past three seasons. On the other side, Jack Eichel's profile continues to grow as one of the league's top players; he has six points through the first three games.

Florida Panthers at Los Angeles Kings

10 p.m. ET (ESPN) | FLA -125, O/U: 5.5

The Panthers will be happy to see their trip through California end, as they lost captain Aleksander Barkov to injury in a loss to the Sharks, then fell short against the Ducks as well. The good news for the Kings: They scored four goals in each of their first two games, which is usually enough to win. The bad news: They allowed eight and five goals, respectively, in those contests, resulting in an 0-1-1 record heading into this showdown.

stories.headline: State of each position in 2026: What are the biggest tactical trends?
stories.summary: Elite soccer has changed dramatically in recent years, and the most valued player skill sets have evolved as a result.
stories.body:
Elite European soccer in 2026 feels decidedly different from what we've become used to. Over the past couple of seasons, the Premier League has been increasingly characterized by direct attacking, set pieces and long throw-ins. Many encounters between big clubs across Europe have become frenetic, end-to-end affairs, such as the Bayern Munich-Paris Saint-Germain semifinals in last season's UEFA Champions League.

A lot of the changes seem related to how teams play without the ball. The soccer we became accustomed to throughout the 2010s involved top sides trying to push their opponents back while keeping the ball. Once the ball reached the attacking third, they tried to outnumber defenders in key spaces and make use of their attacking talent.

One way for defensive sides to counter this approach is to use zonal marking, which involves defending space rather than individual players. They would set up in compact blocks and deny space in critical areas, whether they defended deep like Max Allegri's Juventus in the 2010s or pressed high like teams coached by Ralf Rangnick's disciples. While this tactic helps protect the areas closer to goal and prevent mismatches, it sometimes plays into the hands of those high-possession sides.

As a result, player marking (or man-to-man marking), in which defenders are assigned to follow attackers around up and down the pitch, started to make a comeback at the turn of the 2020s. Teams like Mikel Arteta's Arsenal and Andoni Iraola's Bournemouth combined this concept with their zonal marking, switching out of a zonal structure in certain situations to swarm teams attempting to move the ball forward (hybrid pressing). This makes moving the ball slowly up the pitch harder, causing teams to embrace more direct approaches with the ball.

Meanwhile, the game appears to be becoming more physical and more intense. Since the COVID-19 pandemic, every passing season of the Premier League has seen faster sprinting and more "high-intensity actions." And with off-ball physical data like running distance or top speed becoming more accessible, scouting departments now possess more transparent measures of athleticism, leading to players' athletic qualities being valued more.

Rather than just affecting the head coach's team talk, these big-picture changes have a major effect on the skill sets that clubs look for when assembling their starting XIs. Let's take a look at five positions -- goalkeepers, center backs, fullbacks, central midfielders, and strikers -- to see what has changed and why.

Goalkeepers: Distribution and cross-claiming

New Aston Villa goalkeeper Zion Suzuki has generated much buzz this season. One of his standout features has been his passing ability, playing quick passes to his center backs during the early buildup and exquisite floated long passes to Villa's forwards to escape pressure.

As impressive as his reflex saves are, Suzuki doesn't appear to be a great shot stopper. His "goals prevented" stats, based on post-shot expected goals, reveal that his shot-stopping numbers have hovered around that of the average major league goalkeeper over the past couple of seasons. In fact, in 2025-26, he prevented minus-0.4 goals per 90 minutes, implying that he did slightly worse than the average keeper last season.

However, his passing displays and his excellent cross-claiming make him a highly prized player, and his skill set epitomizes the state of today's goalkeeping.

When Pep Guardiola's Manchester City signed Gianluigi Donnarumma -- known for his shot-stopping abilities, but arguably an average distributor -- as their first-choice goalkeeper in summer 2025, it looked like elite soccer was once again prioritizing shot-stopping between the sticks. But the tactical conditions of soccer in the 2020s make ball-playing goalkeepers even more crucial than before; when teams are tasked with playing the ball past intense man-to-man presses, goalkeepers have more to do in the buildup phase.

Even the most aggressive man-to-man presses don't generally mark the goalkeeper, making keepers free options in the buildup. From this point, keepers are instrumental to playing quick passes around the box to try to bait the press for "artificial transitions" as well as with playing longer passes into space to relieve pressure and kick-start a direct attack.

As a result, the heyday of keepers primarily known for what they can do with their feet looks unlikely to recede anytime soon, with more intense pressing and more direct attacking arguably magnifying their value.

Meanwhile, although the number of open-play crosses that teams in the Big Five leagues play has decreased slightly since 2018, the ever-rising threat of set-play goals makes cross-claiming an especially valuable skill. The first-choice keepers at big clubs dominate the top of the leaderboard for cross-claiming statistics; Donnarumma ranked No. 1 for the highest percentage of crosses claimed in the Premier League last season, Barcelona's Joan García and Real Madrid's Thibaut Courtois ranked second and third, respectively, in last season's LaLiga campaign, and PSG's Lucas Chevalier ranked third in Ligue 1.

On the other hand, the keepers who populated the bottom of cross-claiming tables belong to either lower-table clubs or underperforming established sides like Tottenham Hotspur and Newcastle United. As valuable as goalkeepers' distribution is in 2026, it appears that the ability to claim crosses has become crucial to success between the sticks.

Center backs: Playmaking and pushing forward

In the 2015-16 Premier League season, the top five players who completed the most passes per 90 were Santi Cazorla, Cesc Fabregas, Bastian Schweinsteiger, Aaron Ramsey and Michael Carrick, with more central and attacking midfielders completing the top 10. In 2025-26, the top five were Rodri, Lewis Dunk, Curtis Jones, Trevoh Chalobah and William Saliba, with seven center backs making up the top 10.

A decade ago, central midfielders were at the heart of elite sides' passing moves, but today, especially in the Premier League, center backs are the primary passers in most sides.

In the Big Five leagues, center backs completed 19% more passes in the 2025-26 season than in 2018-19. Much of this has to do with intense man-to-man pressing systems, meaning that players positioned deeper have more prominent buildup duties. The 2020s have also seen nominal center backs become more involved in attacking play, taking up higher and wider positions. Attacking center backs are effective tools to dismantle mid-blocks, helping complicate marking duties with their movement.

This is easiest to do with wide center backs in a back three. Gian Piero Gasperini's Atalanta and Simone Inzaghi's Internazionale did this especially often. This season, Xabi Alonso's Chelsea and Gasperini's AS Roma are key examples, with the latter probably representing the most adventurous iteration of attacking center backs we've seen this century.

We can see some of this in back-four systems, too. Guardiola used John Stones as a center back who roved forward in possession at City, while Thiago Motta used Riccardo Calafiori and Jhon Lucumí as center backs with free roles.

As this decade progresses, the phrase "center back" might be encased in quotation marks more often.

Fullbacks: Rise of the underlap

Fullbacks often epitomize the tactical eras they find themselves in. The turn of the 2010s saw the rise of overlapping attacking fullbacks who move high up the pitch and outside wingers who cut inside with the ball. The mid-to-late 2010s saw the rise of high-intensity pressing, with high-possession sides using inverted fullbacks to provide security against counterattacks resulting from losing the ball. Meanwhile, the relative conservatism that followed the COVID-19 pandemic meant that nominal center backs were often deployed at fullback.

Today, we're seeing the rise of attacking fullbacks who underlap, making runs into the channels between opposition fullbacks and center backs, much like inverted wingers. As Caleb Gearty notes for SCOUTED, "the ability to receive the ball" is progressively becoming more highly valued for fullbacks. After getting in behind back lines, underlapping fullbacks can put in dangerous cutbacks and crosses from closer to goal, or take shots themselves.

In the case of back-three formations, this isn't a new phenomenon. For instance, Thomas Tuchel's Chelsea saw wingbacks Reece James and Ben Chilwell move inside and score goals, while Inzaghi used Federico Dimarco and Denzel Dumfries as goal-scoring threats at Inter.

But now, fullbacks in back-four systems are increasingly venturing forward and inside -- not just putting crosses in, but getting on the end of goal-scoring opportunities, too. Arsenal's Calafiori and Manchester City's Nico O'Reilly often make darting runs into the box and offer secondary goal threats. Spain's World Cup win saw Marc Cucurella and Pedro Porro underlap, pulling defenses apart.

Meanwhile, back-three systems feature wingbacks who pose greater goal-scoring threats than ever. Alonso's Chelsea are an instructive example -- they signed Pep Chavarría and Marco Palestra, but Alonso currently appears to favor the left-footed winger Pedro Neto at right wingback, who makes sharp runs into the box.

Why is this the case? In an age when defensive tactics are dominated by player-marking, the positional interchanges around the flanks (or "wide rotations") and unexpected diagonal darts forward from fullbacks can scramble player-marking duties and open up space -- especially when wingers find themselves closer to the sideline. As Billy Carpenter writes, sudden moves into the spaces in behind defenses can expose structural vulnerabilities in even the best mid-blocks.

Calafiori so far this season represents a great example, making well-timed runs in behind and receiving incisive through balls ...

... and creating goals like these.

Jamie Carragher once remarked that fullbacks are either failed wingers or failed center backs. The rise of inverted fullbacks would've allowed Carragher to add "failed midfielder" to his jibe, while today, a middling inside forward can consider a successful career as an underlapping attacking fullback.

Central midfielders: Large spaces and generalists

In 2026, the most expensive player archetype to sign in soccer appears to be the generalist midfielder. Of the 10 most expensive transfers this summer per Transfermarkt, six were central midfielders. And among the major moves in midfield that big clubs made this summer, most midfielders are do-it-all generalists who, at least in theory, contribute to passing, carrying, winning the ball back and sometimes crashing the box. These include Elliot Anderson, Sandro Tonali, Ayyoub Bouaddi, Bruno Guimarães, Carlos Baleba and Andrey Santos.

This hasn't always been the case. By 2009, the box-to-box midfielder had become a dying breed, superseded by specialists in midfield. In the late 2010s, the rise of pressing meant that press-resistant ball carriers in midfield became increasingly valued, epitomized by the summer 2019 transfer window, which saw Frenkie de Jong, Tanguy Ndombele and Mateo Kovacic move for sums exceeding €40 million. But now, every big club is willing to spend astronomic sums on their own equivalent of Declan Rice or Moisés Caicedo; athletic midfielders who can cover lots of ground and do a bit of everything.

Counterintuitively, this might be happening because less of the game is happening in midfield. With the rise of situational player-marking, the middle third sees larger spaces opened up between lines of pressure, while space becomes more constricted in teams' own thirds. As a result, moving the ball from defense to midfield becomes a harder task, while the spaces opened up in the middle third mean teams don't pass the ball around as much there, instead moving the ball through it more quickly.

Jon Mackenzie and Jake Entwistle have discussed the relevance of "small spaces" -- where the player on the ball has little room to work with in the face of pressure -- and "large spaces" -- where players need to cover ground quickly, especially during transitions or when a line of pressure is broken -- in midfield, which influences how midfielder profiles are valued today. A player like Anderson, who combines small-space and large-space skills, becomes priceless, but the broader emphasis shifts from small-space specialists to large-space generalists who can cover ground and offer control in the center of the park.

As a result, affecting the pace of the attack, rather than just exerting control over space, becomes a key consideration in midfield. The rise of artificial transitions in response to pressing also means central midfielders are key to moving the ball from small spaces to large spaces, as Carlos Baleba did adeptly while at Brighton.

The middle of the park is integral to controlling a game of soccer, and as we're seeing the very notion of "control" change in the middle of the 2020s, the traits associated with the most highly valued midfielders are transformed, too.

Strikers: Physicality and pinning

While the first two decades of top-level soccer in the 21st century saw increasing versatility at the center forward position, the opposite is happening in the third decade. So far, the 2020s have seen taller, faster and stronger strikers being valued more than their smaller, more technical counterparts. Of course, Erling Haaland represents the platonic ideal of a striker -- in this era and in any other -- but the players who spearhead attacks in the middle of the 2020s tend to be 6-foot-2 or taller, and combine their size with pace.

Today's strikers are also less involved in link-up play than their equivalents at the turn of the 2020s, with the average striker in the Big Five leagues completing 16% fewer passes in 2025-26 than in 2018-19.

As discussed earlier, with attacks becoming more direct, the established strategy of pushing teams back and overwhelming defenses with patient play in the attacking third is falling out of fashion, which means strikers don't need to be as involved outside the penalty area. Instead, strikers increasingly spend most of the game pinning back defenders and stretching back lines, attempting to find space within settled defensive blocks. Plus, an increased emphasis on transitions correspondingly makes outlets to hit on the break becoming more valuable, and some extra size certainly comes in handy while trying to score goals from set pieces.

However, the players who currently lead most big clubs' front lines indicate the trend might be reversing at the upper echelons of the game. Harry Kane drops deeper than ever and conducts passing moves from midfield at Bayern, PSG won the Champions League with Ousmane Dembélé as a false 9 last season, Mikel Arteta appears to favor Kai Havertz up front over Viktor Gyokeres at Arsenal, and Barcelona currently deploy Raphinha at the No. 9 spot.

This might be because teams are finding alternate ways of manipulating player-marking strategies, picking holes in defenses with positional interchanges. By dropping deeper, a striker can bring the defender assigned to marking him along and create space for teammates. For example, in this case, João Pedro dropping deep to receive a throw-in pokes a hole for Morgan Rogers to run into, who in turn creates space for Cole Palmer's carry and goal.

For now, specialized, physically gifted strikers may have their time in the sun, but we're likely to see many approaches at the center forward position as the decade progresses.

What to make of 2026 trends

Many soccer fans view today's tactical landscape as being one of stasis or even regression. It's tempting to view the rise of directness and set pieces, as well as do-it-all midfielders and big strikers, as the return of older approaches. But this might be a reductive view; as Mackenzie notes in his book "The Spectre of Pep," presenting changes in the tactical landscape as purely being "cyclical" makes it "very difficult to speak of the 'new' in any meaningful way at all."

All the smaller tactical shifts we're seeing across the pitch are happening in relation to broader changes in the tactical environment of the 2020s. With the rise of man-to-man pressing approaches and the resulting revival of direct attacking, accompanied with the resurgence of ground-eating midfielders and big, physical strikers, these very same trends have brought about the rise of playmaking goalkeepers, attacking center backs, and underlapping fullbacks.

If a Premier League manager from 2006 drove a plutonium-powered DeLorean to 2026, he might find the first five minutes of play recognizable, but would be scandalized by the time he reaches the 10-minute mark. Welcome to elite soccer in the 2020s.

stories.headline: What's next: Will Silva's first title defense be against Shevchenko?
stories.summary: The most likely opponent and a wild card for the winners and losers on the UFC 332 main card.
stories.body:
The UFC has a new women's flyweight champion for the first time in over two years following the UFC 332 main event in Salt Lake City on Saturday night. And with a new champion comes brand-new matchups. After winning the belt via unanimous decision over Wang Cong, Natalia Silva will have no shortage of challengers looking for their shot at gold.

Also on the UFC 332 fight card, rising men's bantamweight contender Payton Talbott made quick work of former two-time men's flyweight champion Deiveson Figueiredo in the co-main event. Talbott could take on a top-ranked contender in his next Octagon appearance. And a handful of young prospects earned impressive first-round knockout victories.

Here's what's next for the top stars of UFC 332.

Natalia Silva, women's flyweight champion

Who should be next: Valentina Shevchenko

The state of the UFC's women's divisions is not ideal. We haven't seen a bantamweight title fight all year, due to injuries to Kayla Harrison. Mackenzie Dern is the strawweight champion, but (fair or not) there is a pretty significant need for her to fight Zhang Weili to validate her standing as the top 115-pound fighter in the world, since Zhang vacated her belt, never lost it in competition. Now the same is true of the flyweight title. Silva has the longest active win streak at 125 pounds and might be the best in the world, but she'll battle for that perception until she fights Shevchenko. We'll have to see how long Shevchenko is out, but this fight needs to happen as soon as possible.

Wild card: Erin Blanchfield

Blanchfield has looked like future champion material since she debuted with the UFC at 22 years old in 2021. She's now five years into her UFC career, and she is 8-1 with one learning experience in the form of a five-round decision loss to Manon Fiorot in 2024. She's still only 27 and could well prove to be the future of this weight class. She's got a tough matchup scheduled against Jasmine Jasudavicius on Oct. 17. If she gets past that unscathed, the UFC could easily book her with Silva as soon as possible, instead of waiting for Shevchenko.

Payton Talbott, men's bantamweight
Who should be next: Sean O'Malley

It has to be done. O'Malley was once the darling of the bantamweight division. Now it's Talbott, and it's hard to deny this matchup. Now, the UFC is almost certainly already looking at O'Malley for an upcoming title fight. Especially if Petr Yan defeats Merab Dvalishvili at UFC 333 later this month, O'Malley is the favorite to face Yan next. But if UFC fans were polled, the more anticipated fight might honestly be O'Malley vs. Talbott. Not to get out of control here, but this could headline a numbered event.

Wild card: Farid Basharat

This would be the anti-O'Malley booking. The UFC doesn't love that Basharat has mostly decisions on his record -- so much so that there's been some uncertainty about his security with the promotion. He's ranked in the top 10 by the UFC but in a spot to defend his spot (not attack). This is the kind of athlete who might need to fight down the rankings. Enter Talbott.

Ateba Gautier, middleweight
Who should be next: Loser of Bo Nickal vs. Joe Pyfer on Dec. 12

Hear me out: Gautier's hype train took a major, major hit with the first-round knockout loss to Roman Kopylov. There's no way around it. He took a step up in competition, and fell very flat. In this situation, the UFC can quietly step him back to the prelims somewhere -- or it can create a story. Gautier's stock took a hit but he is still extremely dangerous. There's still intrigue attached to him. Nickal is coming off a strong win at the White House over Kyle Daukaus, but there are still question marks around him. Pyfer is riding high after a finish of Israel Adesanya in his last bout. Whoever loses between Nickal and Pyfer would still be in position for a compelling bout. What's more compelling than this? There is still a way for the UFC to use what's left of the hype around Gautier and make a fight fans will want to watch.

Wild card: Loser of Daukaus vs. Marc-Andre Barriault on Oct. 17

This would be an appropriate next step that would teach us more about Gautier. Kopylov is a legitimate (for lack of a better word) gatekeeper, and Daukaus and Andre Barriault are also proven veterans. Either would challenge Gautier and offer him a chance at redemption.

stories.headline: Five grand finalists named in Samoa's RLWC squad
stories.summary: Ben Gardiner has been denied the chance to call up Payne Haas, but Samoa's Rugby League World Cup squad remains filled with NRL talent.
stories.body:
Francis Manuleleua and Jermaine McEwen have been rewarded for their starring roles in Newcastle's run to the NRL Grand Final with the back-row duo named in Samoa's Rugby League World Cup squad.

Even without Payne Haas, as the South Sydney-bound prop undergoes hand surgery, the Samoan squad is still packed with talent.

Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Brian To'o and Stephen Crichton are all included, along with Sydney Roosters front-rower Spencer Leniu following his exploits in the NRL Grand Final.

Jarome Luai will co-captain the side with Parramatta prop Junior Paulo.

"One of the great things rugby league does is bring people together," Toa Samoa coach Ben Gardiner said.

"As we build towards our first World Cup game, we want to thank all Samoans around the world for their ongoing support.

"Your blessings and prayers are welcomed.

"Whether you are in Samoa, elsewhere around the world, taking part in a parade or marching into the ground, we see you and thank you for your love and support."

Roosters hooker Benaiah Ioelu is likely to share hooking duties with Jazz Tevaga, who won the Super League Grand Final with Wakefield last week.

Gardiner's side will open their campaign against France in Parramatta before facing Papua New Guinea in Port Moresby and rounding out their pool stage fixtures against Tonga.

Samoa squad: Shawn Blore, Stephen Crichton, Sua Fa'alogo, Clayton Faulalo, Chanel Harris-Tavita, Benaiah Ioelu, Connelly Lemuelu, Spencer Leniu, Jarome Luai, Francis Manuleleua, Deine Mariner, Ata Mariota, Greg Marzhew, Jermaine McEwen, Francis Molo, Junior Paulo, Pasami Saulo, Hamiso Tabuai-Fidow, Izack Tago, Jazz Tevaga, Brian To'o, Enari Tuala, Ronald Volkman.

stories.headline: Predicting how new NBA lottery, anti-tanking rules will impact 2026-27 season
stories.summary: How could the changes aimed at circumventing tanking likely affect on-court outcomes this season?
stories.body:
This NBA season, for the first time, teams can't win by losing. After a tanktastic 2025-26 campaign, the league has instituted a new draft lottery setup with several new features, including:

Flat lottery odds for the teams with the fourth- through 10th-worst records
A "relegation zone" in which the three worst teams get worse odds of landing a top pick
A lottery that draws each of the first 16 picks, rather than just the first four from the old system

This new setup will invariably produce plenty of ripple effects as teams respond to new incentives with new behaviors. Exactly how much things will change, and how these anti-tanking measures might alter transactional decisions such as the trade and buyout markets, remains to be seen.

But for now, here are five predictions for how the new rules will affect on-court outcomes in the 2026-27 season.

Fewer blowouts
In the 2025-26 regular season, 281 games were decided by at least 20 points, which broke the record of 259 set just one year earlier ... which broke the record of 235 set just one year before that ... which broke the record of 232 set just two years before that.

On a percentage basis, last season set a record, too. On a percentage basis, last season set a record, too, as 22% of games were blowouts. If you rank every season in NBA history by the proportion of games decided by 20-plus points, five of the top six have come since 2021.

While the leaguewide blowout rate remained relatively consistent through the first 70-plus years of NBA history, it has skyrocketed in the 2020s.

Several factors explain this sudden rise, including the increased variance of 3-pointers and a general rise in offense; it's easier to win by 20 points when the average team scores 115 points per game instead of 95. But when scoring was also high in the 1960s and 1980s, blowout rates in those decades weren't close to where they are now.

Instead, it appears that teams' modern approach to late-season games has skewed competitiveness. The NBA's blowout rate increased considerably as the 2025-26 season went on, especially in games involving tanking teams. From the start of February through the end of the season, a full third of games involving the NBA's worst teams ended with at least a 20-point margin.

Now that the league's cellar-dwellers no longer have an incentive to keep losing -- and in fact might have an incentive to win games to avoid the relegation zone -- the blowout rate should theoretically stop spiking in February, March and April.

Broader increases in competitiveness could also make the league's best teams look a little less dominant. In the 2024-25 season, when the Thunder set an NBA record with a plus-12.9 point differential, they received a big boost from competition that wasn't trying to win. The Thunder were plus-10.5 against non-tanking teams and a whopping plus-22.6 against that season's tankers, with five of their seven largest wins -- which were all by 33 points or more -- coming against teams that preferred to lose.

A relatively unchanged offensive environment
One of my first impulses when brainstorming the potential ripple effects of the new lottery rules was that scoring might decrease across the league, on average, now that there won't be uncompetitive defenses to torch on a nightly basis.

One of last season's standout games was the Miami Heat's 150-129 win over the Washington Wizards on March 10, as Bam Adebayo scored 83 points against the worst team in the league.

Zooming out, the NBA's bottom nine defenses last season all belonged to teams that lost 50-plus games. And the three worst defenses were the Wizards, Jazz and Kings, who all lost at least 60 games while allowing more than 120 points per 100 possessions. According to Stathead, those teams had the three highest defensive ratings in NBA history.

Indeed, if you remove the six teams that seemed to most desperately want losses by the end of last season -- the Wizards, Pacers, Nets, Jazz, Kings and Grizzlies -- the average of the other 24 teams' defensive ratings would have improved by 1.2 points.

But at the same time, the average offensive rating would have improved by a similar 1.0 points.

After all, the three worst offensive ratings last season belonged to the Nets, Wizards and Pacers, who all lost more than 60 games, as well. And the nine worst offenses belonged to teams that lost 50-plus games, too.

It turns out that not trying to win made teams almost equally bad at both offense and defense, so forcing all those teams to flip a switch should have a relatively neutral effect on leaguewide offensive totals.

More compressed standings
As some teams raced to accumulate as many losses as possible last season -- all for the purpose of improving their lottery odds -- their opponents who wished to make the playoffs all picked up plenty of "free" wins. Fittingly, a record 19 teams finished with winning records last season.

For some of those teams that snuck above .500, that feat was only possible because they beat up on the league's worst teams. The Trail Blazers, for instance, won just 41% of their games against non-tanking opposition, but went 16-2 against the six bottom-feeders to finish 42-40 overall. The 76ers won 44% of their games against other opponents but went 17-1 against the tankers, en route to a 45-37 finish. The Clippers, Hornets, Suns, Heat, Hawks, Magic and Raptors all went from below-.500 to above because they racked up wins against teams that weren't really trying to beat them.

And even if there will always be vast differences between the NBA's wheat and chaff in any given season, those gaps shouldn't be as extreme under the new lottery setup. Even if the bottom six teams had all won just five more games apiece last season -- meaning they still would have lost 50-plus games and been well outside the playoff picture -- there would have been 30 fewer wins to go around for the teams in the middle and top of the standings.

Put another way, the 37-45 Warriors were the only team that finished with between 32 and 43 wins last season. There will likely be many more teams stuck in that middle ground this year.

More familiar late-season rosters
One of the main ways that teams have tried to plummet down the standings is to shut down their stars and rely on unproven, relatively anonymous players down the stretch. That practice reached overdrive last season.

Out of the 11 players on the Jazz and Grizzlies who averaged at least 30 minutes per game in April, seven were on 10-day contracts: Utah's Bez Mbeng and Kennedy Chandler, and Memphis' Rayan Rupert, Toby Okani, Lucas Williamson, Dariq Whitehead and Adama Bal. Also in April, two-way player Ethan Thompson led the Pacers in minutes, while Malachi Smith (on a 10-day contract) and Tyson Etienne (on a two-way contract) led the Nets.

Under the new lottery structure, however, teams won't need to resort to such roster shenanigans to improve their lottery odds by fractions of percentage points. They might still prefer to ramp up youngsters' playing time in March and April as they focus more on development, but that shift should be much subtler now, and involve actual prospects rather than fungible, fringe NBA talent on 10-day deals.

That change will hurt the Mbengs and Ruperts of the world, who won't have a route to 30 minutes a night anymore. But it's probably a win for fans who will be more familiar with, and connected to, the players they're watching.

Some teams still not trying to win, regardless
Despite the NBA's best efforts, it's unlikely that all 30 teams will have a steadfast devotion to winning every game this season. The problem is that some of the squads with the worst projections don't control their own 2027 first-round selections, so they won't have the same strong motivation to clinch the best lottery odds.

The Clippers owe their pick, via swap, to the Thunder. The Bucks owe their pick to the Pelicans or Hawks. And the Nets owe their pick, via swap, to the Rockets. If those teams linger near the bottom of the standings, they won't have any reason to win frequently enough to escape the relegation zone.

If anything, a non-playoff team that doesn't control its own pick might be incentivized to lose to stay in the relegation zone. Beyond the reconfiguration of the lottery odds, the new rules also prohibit teams from winning back-to-back lotteries or picking inside the top five for three consecutive drafts, which could encourage bad behavior.

Let's use the Nets as an example. If Brooklyn is a run-of-the-mill bad team this season, it could land the No. 1 pick but have to send it to Houston, and then be prevented from landing the top pick again in 2028. However, if the Nets target the relegation zone, their odds of winning the No. 1 pick in 2027 will be lower, which could benefit them in future lotteries when they control their own pick again.

That sort of double-reverse tanking possibility won't be nearly as common or widespread as more straightforward tanking motivations in the past, but it still lingers. All in all, the new lottery system will likely produce more competitive, watchable basketball down the stretch this spring -- but it won't be a perfect solution right away.

stories.headline: Is Bijan Robinson the NFL's top RB? He is when he's in primetime
stories.summary: Bijan Robinson has the most scrimmage yards per game in primetime, and he'll get a chance to keep it rolling on 'Monday Night Football' this week.
stories.body:
Editor's note: This originally ran Monday morning, before Atlanta Falcons running back Bijan Robinson rushed for 145 yards and two touchdowns in a 45-24 rout of the New Orleans Saints. Robinson now has averaged 145.5 scrimmage yards in primetime, the most ever for a RB with a minimum of five games.

FLOWERY BRANCH, Ga. -- Atlanta Falcons coach Kevin Stefanski shows high school football highlights of his players to the team on Fridays. For most, the glory days of high school set a bar few could match against NFL competition.

Then there's Bijan Robinson.

To be clear, Robinson was a superstar at Salpointe Catholic High School in Tucson, Arizona. He was the Gatorade Player of the Year as a senior in 2019. But Robinson's highlights on Friday nights don't match what he has done under the lights in the NFL.

Since the 1970 NFL/AFC merger, no player has more scrimmage yards per game in primetime than Robinson (145.4 in 11 games) with a minimum of five games, per ESPN Research. Barry Sanders is second with 126.3 scrimmage yards per game in 20 contests. OJ Simpson (123 in six games) and Jonathan Taylor (121.8 in 12 games) are third and fourth, respectively.

Robinson will try to keep it rolling Monday when the Falcons (1-2) travel to New Orleans (1-2) to face the Saints (8:15 p.m. ET, ESPN).

"For me, whether it's primetime, whether it's a 1 o'clock game, they're all the same in terms of my mentality," Robinson said. "Everybody watches you on TV, and they watch you in the stands.

"I love what Kobe [Bryant] said: 'They paid to watch you, so you got to do your job on the field.'"

Robinson was remarkable against the Green Bay Packers on "Thursday Night Football" in Week 3, leading Atlanta to a 35-14 road win. He had 29 carries for 194 yards and two touchdowns, and added another 19 yards on two receptions.

"He's an elite player," Packers head coach Matt LaFleur said. "He's one of the best in the league at any position." The Falcons signed Robinson to an offseason extension that briefly made him the highest-paid running back in NFL history. Robinson, the No. 8 pick in the 2023 draft, is under contract for three years with a base salary of $66.75 million ($22.3 million per season), which could go up to $75 million. The Detroit Lions' Jahmyr Gibbs has the highest average per year at $22.5 million.

"Bro, I don't know what to say," Packers running back Kaleb Johnson said after the Week 3 game. "He deserves every penny of that."

Robinson has picked up where he left off in 2025, when he was named first-team All-Pro. He once again leads the league in yards from scrimmage (467) and is second in rushing yards (349).

Last season, he had the two longest runs of his career -- 93 yards against the Los Angeles Rams and 81 yards against the Buffalo Bills -- on "Monday Night Football." Against the Minnesota Vikings on "Sunday Night Football" in 2025, Robinson had 168 scrimmage yards. Since Robinson debuted in 2023, he has over 20 scrimmage yards per game more than any other running back in primetime. More than Derrick Henry (123.9). More than Saquon Barkley (119.5).

In his past four primetime games, Robinson is averaging 213.8 scrimmage yards. Robinson can't explain why he has excelled in primetime. He said he's not necessarily a night person, usually going to sleep around 11 p.m. "When it's time to [play], no matter what time it is, it's time to go," Robinson said. "So, the game can be played at 12 midnight, and I'm locked in, ready to go."

That same mentality is evident when Stefanski shows high school clips of Robinson.

"Our players love playing under the lights, and that takes all of us back to high school days and Friday night lights," Stefanski said. "And every Friday team meeting, I show high school highlights of one of our players.

"We've done Bijan before, so I've seen what it looked like [under] Friday night lights out there in Arizona. It was pretty special."

Even more so against the best players in the world. It's enough for recently acquired defensive tackle Gervon Dexter Sr. to put an exclamation mark on the praise. "He's the best player I've ever seen play football."

stories.headline: 2026 MLB playoffs: How Fernando Tatis Jr. got his groove back
stories.summary: If they're going to mount an NLDS comeback, the Pads will need to mirror the perseverance of their biggest star.
stories.body:
WITH TWO HEARTBREAKS behind him and a mountain ahead of him, San Diego Padres manager Craig Stammen was asked about the challenge of taking three consecutive National League Division Series games against the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers. He pointed to the regular season, during which the Padres went from floundering in July to percolating in August to dominating by September.

"We've been resilient all year," Stammen said before a Monday workout at Petco Park, ahead of Tuesday's Game 3. "We've had our backs against the wall several times. Players, individually, have had their backs against the wall."

No player represents that better than the Padres' most important one.

Fernando Tatis Jr. did not hit his first home run until May 30 and somehow finished with 25 homers. Fifty games into the Padres' season, he ranked 165th among 171 qualified players in slugging percentage. By the end of it, he was slashing .289/.350/.470.

"It was determination," Tatis said. "It would've been easy just to get carried over by the emotions and say it was a bad year, but, man, we just kept working."

To rediscover his form, Tatis had to tap into old mechanics and overhaul his swing. He had to lean on a former hitting coach and a future Hall of Famer. Mostly, though, Tatis had to pick himself up and rally like never before. He went from looking like a lost cause to putting together what he believes is the best stretch of his life, a mesmerizing two-month surge that coincided with the Padres' rise.

The apex occurred in the Padres' postseason opener seven days ago, in front of a sold-out, frenzied Petco Park crowd, when Tatis hit the first pitch he saw 405 feet for a leadoff home run and later raced home to score on an attempted steal of second base.

Since then, Tatis is 1-for-14. And though the two losses in Milwaukee were defined by Ty France's roof-interrupted fly ball and Mason Miller's blown save, the reality is the Padres scored just five runs and went 3-for-18 with runners in scoring position against the Brewers' pitchers. Since the division series moved to its current 2-2-1 format, only three of the 36 teams that lost the first two games on the road won the series. For the Padres to become the fourth, their offense will have to get going.

And that starts with Tatis.

As Padres shortstop Xander Bogaerts said: "He goes, we go."

TATIS WENT 2-FOR-4 with a grand slam in a pool play game against Israel on March 9, lifting his OPS to 1.567 through the first three games of the World Baseball Classic. The next day, when the Dominican team reconvened for a workout, Tatis was toying with a new approach. Albert Pujols, his manager for the international tournament, couldn't believe it.

"He changes a lot, man," Pujols said in Spanish. "And that affects him a lot."

Making constant tweaks, often unnecessarily, has been a common theme, one he readily acknowledges, throughout Tatis' career. Tatis is supremely athletic, with ample range of motion. But sometimes, he said, those traits can be "a curse."

"I'm able to do all these things," Tatis said. "But at the same time, it's: How do you pick which one is going to work at the moment?"

When the regular season began, Tatis chose a closed stance, one he had experimented with from time to time over the past few years. He wanted to limit the moving parts of his load, make his swing more efficient and give himself a chance to hit for a higher batting average. Instead, Tatis said, "My body was just getting stuck with my swing. I was getting off my back foot. I wasn't loading and separating in a way that would benefit me to hit the ball the right way."

Tatis produced elite exit velocities through the season's first two months, but he was beating pitches into the ground and hardly lifting them to his pull side. It was the middle of May. His batting average was in the low .200s, his slugging percentage was among the lowest in the sport and his home run total was stuck at zero.

It was around then that Pujols checked in.

"That kid was so down, man," Pujols said. "It was ugly. And that worried me a lot. And that's why I started communicating more with him."

Fourteen years ago, Pujols went through something similar. He had signed a 10-year, $240 million contract with the Los Angeles Angels, then put together one of the best spring training performances he could remember. But when the games started to count, he lost his swing. Pujols didn't hit his first home run in an Angels uniform until May 6. By the end of the year, though, the production was there. It took three months for him to put up the numbers he needed to for an entire season. Pujols relayed that story to Tatis. If I could do it, Pujols told him, so can you.

"The way he talked," Tatis said, "putting me in sentences with his name -- 'players like us, we can do it.' Stuff like that, it can really lift you up."

Tatis needed the confidence boost. But mostly, he needed help with his mechanics. For the better part of two weeks, he communicated with Pujols almost daily. Tatis would send him video, and Pujols would send him more, often putting together split screens of Tatis' old swing side by side with his current one. Pujols wanted Tatis to focus on loading into his back leg.

"He was hitting the ball hard because he's strong," Pujols said. "But his hips weren't working the way they're supposed to. He was using too much of his upper body. And sometimes, that also makes you late to the ball. He'd hit it hard, but he was late. And he was fouling off balls that he normally would put in the seats."

By May 30, 393 players had hit a home run, and Tatis was not one of them. In the fifth inning of that night's game in Washington, D.C., right-hander Foster Griffin threw a 91 mph fastball low and in and Tatis drove it 451 feet, raising his hands in celebration and relief. It was his first home run, but also his 13th hit in a stretch of 23 at-bats. He was generating power with his lower half again. His swing was better equipped for pulling pitches into the air.

Not long after that, Pujols called to tell him he would circle back in three months.

"Don't let me go!" Tatis told him.

"Nah," Pujols recalled saying, "we'll talk in September. Your numbers will be there."

TATIS STILL WASN'T a finished product. And nobody knew that better than Raúl Padrón. Before being promoted to the major league coaching staff this offseason, Padrón spent 10 years in the Padres' minor league system making various stops as a hitting coach, some of them while Tatis was ascending through the system. In 2018, when a 19-year-old Tatis finished April with a .177 batting average in Double-A, Padrón helped him get back on track. Along the way, he became one of his most trusted advisors.

And so, on May 21, an off day before a weekend home series against the Athletics, Padres general manager A.J. Preller, Stammen and the team's four hitting coaches decided Tatis needed just one voice from the team, and that one voice needed to be Padrón. Seeing results over the next few days, most notably a home run, was encouraging. But throughout June, their work remained. The first task was to open Tatis' stance again, allowing him to reintroduce his higher leg kick.

Said Tatis: "It was all about fluidity."

Padrón's focus wasn't so much on mechanics but rather on helping Tatis "find the rhythm of his body."

"We needed to find a way for the body to work the way it always works -- with his leg kick, opening up a little bit," Padrón said in Spanish. "That gets him a little bit more into his legs, and obviously, the strength is in your legs. He's never been a hitter focused on mechanics. He's always been about rhythm with great IQ in the batter's box. He doesn't need to be thinking about a bunch of things to get a hit."

The extra work in the batting cage continued. The conversations did, too. The results were starting to match. Tatis slashed .318/.356/.509 with four home runs in June, but Padrón wasn't seeing what he needed to yet. Before Tatis departed for the All-Star break, Padrón left him with a thought: Remember to stay loose, especially with your upper body. He told him to stand in front of a mirror and practice it.

By the time the Padres began their second half in Kansas City on the weekend of July 17, Padrón said, "Everything had changed."

"His mind was at peace. He was more relaxed, more willing to take things as they come, whether it was a good result or not. He started to let his talent work for him."

Tatis stayed hot through July and August and took it to another level in September. Only two players, Pete Crow-Armstrong and Pete Alonso, hit more home runs than Tatis' 20 after the All-Star break. He slashed .307/.385/.610 and put up 3.7 FanGraphs wins above replacement, tied for second highest in the majors. Tatis believes it was the best stretch of his career. Many around him agree.

"It would have been easy for him to look up after a couple of months, 'Hey, maybe not my year, maybe not my season,'" Preller said. "There was none of that, no quit from his standpoint. It was, 'I'm going to figure this out.'"

The Padres took off down the stretch, going a major league-best 35-17 in August and September while scoring the third-most runs. Jackson Merrill turned around his season, France became a steady presence in the middle of the lineup, and Dustin Harris, Samad Taylor and Ethan Salas emerged. But the Padres' surge coinciding with Tatis unlocking the best version of himself is no coincidence.

Along the way, Tatis learned something about himself -- something the Padres hope will carry over with their season on the brink.

"That I'm always here," he said. "In this game, I'm never out of it. In a season, in a baseball season, I'm never out of it."

stories.headline: Singapore Grand Prix 2026: Race start time, how to watch, full schedule, predictions
stories.summary: Formula 1's original night race is back as drivers prepare for the ultimate challenge around the Marina Bay Circuit in Singapore.
stories.body:
Formula 1's original night race is back as drivers prepare for the ultimate challenge around the Marina Bay Circuit in Singapore.

It will also be the sixth and final sprint race of the season as Singapore hosts it for the first time.

Max Verstappen claimed his first victory of the season at the Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, while Kimi Antonelli extended his lead in the title championship to 84 points from George Russell.

So you don't miss a thing, here's everything you need to know for the 17th round of the season.

- Bahrain GP was the worst indictment of F1's new engine regs yet

- Could Malaysia return to F1 calendar? The state of play despite Sepang travel chaos

- Max Verstappen wins disrupted Bahrain GP, Kimi Antonelli extends title lead as George Russell retires

Singapore Grand Prix schedule
All times in BST

Friday, October 9

Practice One: 9.30 a.m. - 10.30 a.m.

Sprint Qualifying: 1.30 p.m. - 2.14 p.m.

Saturday, October 10

Sprint: 10 a.m. - 11 a.m.

Qualifying: 2 p.m. - 3 p.m.

Sunday, October 11

Singapore Grand Prix: 1 p.m.

How to watch

Every practice and qualifying session as well as the race itself will be available to watch on Sky Sports F1. The sessions are also on Sky Sports Main Event.

For non-subscribers, highlights of the Singapore Grand Prix will be on free-to-air television on Channel 4.

In the U.S., subscribers can watch every session on Apple TV, via a new F1 channel on the platform.

Marina Bay Street Circuit

Singapore is one of the toughest challenges on the calendar for drivers due to the intense humidity and physically demanding nature of the circuit.

But this time round the drivers will have had a chance to get used to the humid conditions after racing in Malaysia for the Bahrain Grand Prix last weekend.

The Marina Bay Circuit has been on the calendar since 2008 and is one of the standout tracks. The race takes place at night with its breathtaking views of the city's skyline as cars make their way through the tight and twisty circuit.

Drivers can lose around 3kg in body weight after each race due to the amount they sweat.

Singapore Grand Prix

Circuit: Marina Bay Street Circuit; Singapore

Previous winners in Singapore

2014: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2015: Sebastian Vettel (Ferrari)

2016: Nico Rosberg (Mercedes)

2017: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2018: Lewis Hamilton (Mercedes)

2019: Sebastian Vettel (Ferrari)

2022: Sergio Pérez (Red Bull)

2023: Carlos Sainz (Ferrari)

2024: Lando Norris (McLaren)

2025: George Russell (Mercedes)

Other key stats

First F1 race: 2008

Lap record: 1:33.808 Lewis Hamilton (2025)

Most wins: Sebastian Vettel has the most wins with five (2011-2013, 2015 and 2019). From the current grid, Hamilton has four wins (2009, 2014, 2017-2018) and Fernando Alonso with two (2008 and 2010). Pérez (2022), Sainz (2023), Norris (2024) and Russell (2025) have all won a race each here.

Most poles: Vettel (2011, 2013, 2015, 2017) and Hamilton (2009, 2012, 2014, 2018) share the pole record with four each. From the current grid, Charles Leclerc (2019, 2022) has had two pole positions here.

Weather forecast

The weather for the Singapore Grand Prix is set to be thundery showers and light winds throughout the weekend, with highs of 34°C on Friday. The temperature is forecast to drop a degree for the remainder of the weekend.

What happened last time out?
Russell claimed pole position in Singapore last year and crossed the line 0.182 seconds clear of Red Bull's Verstappen, with McLaren's Oscar Piastri behind.

Russell took his second win of the season, but there was plenty of other drama during the race, especially at McLaren.

Norris, who started in fifth, knocked into Piastri when trying to pass him in the first corner. Piastri managed to gain some ground towards the end of the race, but he had to settle for fourth on the day McLaren lifted the trophy for the constructors' title.

Piastri's drivers' championship lead to Norris was separated by only 22 points with six races left of the season.

Who will win this year?

One to watch this weekend is Red Bull and Verstappen after he won the race last weekend. The team brought major upgrades two races ago and improvements to its overall performance has been evident.

Russell, who suffered a major blow to his championship hopes after retiring last time out, will be looking to maximise the points on offer across the weekend.

Mercedes are expected to be strong, while Ferrari are quick in cornering speed. Hamilton has won four times here, so could be a threat. McLaren's Norris and Piastri fell under the radar and struggled for pace in Malaysia.

All will be to play for under the lights in Singapore as we head into the business end of the season.
